paragraphs: “I wouldn’t tell him for anything,” said Alyosha, smiling.
“Ech! You think he’s hurt by it. He’s not. He’s jealous on purpose. He doesn’t care,” said Grushenka bitterly.
“On purpose?” asked Alyosha.

“I’m telling you, Alyosha, you’re silly. For all your cleverness, you know nothing about this. I’m not offended that he’s jealous of a girl like me. I’d be offended if he weren’t. That’s how I am. Jealousy doesn’t offend me. I have a fierce heart myself. I can be jealous too. What offends me is that he doesn’t love me at all. I tell you, he’s jealous now _on purpose_. Am I blind? Can’t I see? Just now he started talking to me about that woman, about Katerina, saying she was this and she was that, how she’d sent for a doctor from Moscow to try to save him, how she’d hired the best lawyer, the most learned one too. So he loves her, if he’ll praise her to my face. Shame on him! He’s treated me badly himself, so he attacked me, to put me in the wrong first and pin it all on me. ‘You were with your Pole before me, so I can’t be blamed over Katerina’—that’s what it comes to. He wants to throw the whole blame on me. He attacked me on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I’ll—”
Grushenka couldn’t finish saying what she would do. She hid her eyes in her handkerchief and sobbed violently.
“He doesn’t love Katerina Ivanovna,” said Alyosha firmly.

“Well, whether he loves her or not, I’ll soon find out for myself,” said Grushenka, with a threatening note in her voice, taking the handkerchief from her eyes. Her face was twisted. Alyosha saw with sorrow that it had gone from mild and calm to sullen and spiteful.

“Enough of this nonsense,” she said suddenly. “That’s not why I sent for you. Alyosha, darling, tomorrow—what will happen tomorrow? That’s what worries me! And it’s only me it worries! I look at everyone, and no one is thinking about it. No one cares. Are you even thinking about it? Tomorrow he’ll be tried, you know. Tell me, how will he be tried? You know it was the valet, the valet who killed him! Good heavens! Can they condemn him in the valet’s place, and will no one stand up for him? They haven’t bothered the valet at all, have they?”

“He’s been cross-examined hard,” Alyosha said thoughtfully, “but everyone came to the conclusion it wasn’t him. Now he’s lying very ill. He’s been ill ever since that attack. Really ill,” Alyosha added.
“Oh, dear! Couldn’t you go to that lawyer yourself and tell him the whole thing? They say he was brought from Petersburg for three thousand roubles.”

“We put up the three thousand together—Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna and I—but she paid the two thousand for the doctor from Moscow herself. The lawyer Fetyukovitch would have charged more, but the case has become known all over Russia. It’s talked about in all the papers and journals. Fetyukovitch agreed to come more for the glory of it, because the case has become so notorious. I saw him yesterday.”
“Well? Did you talk to him?” Grushenka put in eagerly.
“He listened and said nothing. He told me he had already formed his opinion. But he promised to consider my words.”
“Consider them! Ah, they’re swindlers! They’ll ruin him. And why did she send for the doctor?”
“As an expert. They want to prove that Mitya is mad and committed the murder without knowing what he was doing.” Alyosha smiled gently. “But Mitya won’t agree to that.”

“Yes, but it would be the truth if he had killed him!” cried Grushenka. “He was mad then, completely mad, and that was my fault, wretch that I am! But of course he didn’t do it, he didn’t do it! And they’re all against him, the whole town. Even Fenya’s evidence went to show he’d done it. And the people at the shop, and that official, and at the tavern too, before—people had heard him say so! They’re all, all against him, all crying out against him.”
“Yes, there’s a terrible pile of evidence,” Alyosha said grimly.
“And Grigory—Grigory Vassilyevitch—sticks to his story that the door was open. He insists he saw it, and there’s no shaking him. I went and talked to him myself. He was rude about it, too.”
“Yes, that’s perhaps the strongest evidence against him,” said Alyosha.

“And as for Mitya being mad, he certainly seems like it now,” Grushenka began, with a strangely anxious and mysterious air. “Do you know, Alyosha, I’ve wanted to talk to you about it for a long time. I go to him every day and I just wonder at him. Tell me, what do you think he’s always talking about? He talks and talks and I can make nothing of it. I thought he was talking about something intellectual that I couldn’t understand, in my foolishness. Only then he suddenly started talking to me about a babe—that is, some child. ‘Why is the babe poor?’ he said. ‘It’s for that babe that I’m going to Siberia now. I’m not a murderer, but I must go to Siberia!’ What that meant, what babe, I couldn’t tell for the life of me. Only I cried when he said it, because he said it so beautifully. He cried himself, and I cried too. He suddenly kissed me and made the sign of the cross over me. What did it mean, Alyosha? Tell me. What is this babe?”
“It must be Rakitin, who’s been going to see him lately,” Alyosha said with a smile, “though ... that’s not Rakitin’s doing. I didn’t see Mitya yesterday. I’ll see him today.”
“No, it’s not Rakitin. It’s his brother Ivan Fyodorovitch upsetting him. It’s his going to see him, that’s what it is,” Grushenka began, and suddenly broke off. Alyosha stared at her in amazement.
“Ivan goes to see him? Has he been? Mitya told me himself that Ivan hasn’t been once.”

“There ... there! What a girl I am! Blurting things out!” exclaimed Grushenka, confused and suddenly blushing. “Wait, Alyosha, hush! Since I’ve said this much, I’ll tell you the whole truth—he’s been to see him twice. The first time was right when he arrived. He galloped here from Moscow at once, of course, before I fell ill. The second time was a week ago. He told Mitya not to tell you about it under any circumstances, and not to tell anyone, in fact. He came in secret.”
Alyosha sat lost in thought, turning something over. The news had clearly struck him.

“Ivan doesn’t talk to me about Mitya’s case,” he said slowly. “He’s said very little to me these last two months. And whenever I go to see him, he seems annoyed that I’ve come, so I haven’t gone to him for the last three weeks. H’m!... if he was there a week ago ... then there certainly has been a change in Mitya this week.”

“There has been a change,” Grushenka agreed quickly. “They have a secret, they have a secret! Mitya told me himself there was a secret, and such a secret that Mitya can’t rest. Before that he was cheerful—and he is cheerful now, in fact—but when he shakes his head like that, you know, and strides about the room and keeps pulling at the hair on his right temple with his right hand, I know there’s something on his mind, worrying him.... I know! He was cheerful before, though, and he is cheerful today, in fact.”
“But you said he was worried.”

“Yes, he’s worried and yet cheerful. He keeps being irritable for a minute, then cheerful, then irritable again. And you know, Alyosha, I’m always wondering at him—with this awful thing hanging over him, he sometimes laughs at the silliest little things, as if he were a baby himself.”
“And did he really tell you not to tell me about Ivan? Did he say, ‘Don’t tell him’?”

“Yes, he told me, ‘Don’t tell him.’ It’s you Mitya is most afraid of. Because it’s a secret—he said himself it was a secret. Alyosha, darling, go to him and find out what their secret is, and come and tell me,” Grushenka begged him with sudden eagerness. “Put my mind at rest, so that I know the worst that’s in store for me. That’s why I sent for you.”
“You think it has something to do with you? If it did, he wouldn’t have told you there was a secret.”
“I don’t know. Maybe he wants to tell me but doesn’t dare. He’s warning me. There’s a secret, he tells me, but he won’t say what it is.”
“What do you think yourself?”

“What do I think? It’s the end for me, that’s what I think. All three of them have been plotting my end, because Katerina’s in it. It’s all Katerina, it all comes from her. She’s this and she’s that, and that means that I’m not. He tells me so beforehand—warns me. He’s planning to throw me over, that’s the whole secret. They’ve planned it together, the three of them—Mitya, Katerina and Ivan Fyodorovitch. Alyosha, I’ve wanted to ask you for a long time. A week ago he suddenly told me that Ivan was in love with Katerina, because he often goes to see her. Did he tell me the truth or not? Tell me, on your conscience, tell me the worst.”
“I won’t lie to you. Ivan is not in love with Katerina Ivanovna, I think.”

“Oh, that’s what I thought! He’s lying to me, the shameless deceiver, that’s what it is! And he was jealous of me just now so as to put the blame on me afterwards. He’s stupid, he can’t hide what he’s doing. He’s so open, you know.... But I’ll give it to him, I’ll give it to him! ‘You believe I did it,’ he said. He said that to me, to me. He threw that in my face! God forgive him! You wait, I’ll make it hot for Katerina at the trial! I’ll just say one word then ... I’ll tell everything then!”
And again she cried bitterly.

“This I can tell you for certain, Grushenka,” Alyosha said, getting up. “First, that he loves you, loves you more than anyone in the world, and you only, believe me. I know. I do know. The second thing is that I don’t want to worm his secret out of him. But if he tells me of his own accord today, I’ll tell him straight out that I promised to tell you. Then I’ll come to you today and tell you. Only ... I think ... Katerina Ivanovna has nothing to do with it, and the secret is about something else. That’s certain. It doesn’t seem likely to me that it’s about Katerina Ivanovna. Goodbye for now.”

Alyosha shook hands with her. Grushenka was still crying. He saw that she put little faith in his comfort, but she was better for having had her cry out, for having spoken of it. He was sorry to leave her in such a state of mind, but he was in a hurry. He still had a great many things to do.
